_verify: VERIFIED, Rijksmuseum SK-C-230 (The Sick Woman, c. 1663-66, 76 x 63.5 cm): a young woman leans her head on a cushion while a doctor takes her pulse; bed, lute and clock in the background; a stove and a small test at lower left: a quack would put a strip of the patient's clothing in a brazier and the smell would reveal her secret (pregnancy); the doctor's old-fashioned clothes mark him as a comic charlatan. Hektoen International: 'the doctor has placed a piece of the woman's dress in a heated vessel as a test for pregnancy'.
GENERAL (low risk): Steen painted many doctor's-visit scenes; lute as a love symbol is a common Dutch genre convention.

slides.headline: She isn't really sick. Find the clue.
slides.sub: Jan Steen, The Sick Woman, about 1663-66

slides.headline: A house call
slides.text: A Dutch home in the 1660s. A young woman leans weakly on a pillow. The doctor has come, and he takes her pulse very seriously.

slides.headline: The patient
slides.text: She looks pale and tired, her head resting on a cushion. But Steen's buyers would have smiled the moment they saw her.

slides.headline: The doctor
slides.text: Look at his clothes: old-fashioned, almost theatrical. In Steen's time this costume meant one thing: a quack, a comic fake doctor.

slides.headline: The test
slides.text: Down in the corner, a small heated vessel. Inside, a strip of her dress is burning. It is an old folk test.

slides.headline: The secret
slides.text: Quacks claimed the smell of the burning cloth would reveal her condition. She is not ill at all. She is pregnant.

slides.headline: The bed
slides.text: Behind them stands the bed. In Steen's paintings, details like this were jokes the viewer was meant to catch.

slides.headline: Lute and clock
slides.text: Nearby hang a lute, an old symbol of love, and a clock. Time is passing, and soon everyone will know.

slides.headline: Lovesick
slides.text: Steen painted scenes like this again and again, and buyers loved them. The real illness? Love. So who is the father?
